Start · What this tutorial will let you explain

Two compact bodies orbit one another. Gravitational waves carry energy away. Their orbit tightens, their motion speeds up, and a distant observer receives an oscillation that grows in frequency and amplitude: a chirp. We will connect each part of that story to the quantities plotted by GravitationalWaveSources.

Begin with the receiving end of the wave, then build a simple source, then follow its energy. The first four Beats use illustrations and short calculations. Beat 4 opens the Python program. Optional expandable passages supply more algebra; the main explanation does not depend on opening them.

All figures and typeset equations are included in this file. The sliders work locally in a browser without an internet connection. The diagrams exaggerate effects for visibility. No diagram is a measurement of a real event.

Beat 0 · Begin where the wave arrives

Imagine freely falling markers in otherwise nearly empty space. Initially they form a circle. A gravitational wave travels perpendicular to their plane. We can describe its local effect by comparing the distances between markers: while distances along one axis increase, those along the perpendicular axis decrease. Half a cycle later the pattern reverses.

The markers are at the receiving end. They are not the two orbiting objects that generated the wave. The dashed circle is a reference shape; no material ring or elastic connections join the markers.

Normalized component h/H = 1.00. Horizontal span stretched; vertical span squeezed.

This is the receiving end, viewed perpendicular to the wave’s travel. The markers are not the source binary and are not joined by a material ring. Only one polarization component is illustrated.

Try before reading on. Move the phase through a full cycle. At which phases is the horizontal span greatest? When the horizontal span is smallest, what happens to the vertical span? Sketch one positive-strain and one negative-strain arrangement.

Strain describes the fractional stretching and squeezing, rather than an absolute displacement in meters. Its smallness is therefore expressed by a dimensionless number. A strain scale of one part in 1021 is 10−21; it does not mean a displacement of 10−21 meters irrespective of the distance being measured.

The sign identifies which of two perpendicular directions is stretched. Negative strain does not mean negative radiation energy. The figure shows one plus-polarization component. A general wave also has a cross component, whose axes are rotated by 45°. We can understand the plotted representative oscillation without modeling a particular detector’s orientation or response.

How does strain relate to a length change?

For a weak plus-polarized wave and suitably oriented freely falling markers, in the long-wavelength limit, the first-order changes in perpendicular separations are

ΔLxL≃h+2,ΔLyL≃−h+2.

Thus their differential change is (ΔLx−ΔLy)/L≃h+. For an ideal orientation, a strain 10−21 across two 4-km reference arms corresponds to a differential length change of about 4×10−18m. Actual interferometers measure a direction-dependent combination of the two polarizations. The program does not model that detector response.

Read an oscillation before reading a chirp

Three separate ideas will appear in the program:

QuantityPhysical questionVisual clue
Strain h(t)Which deformation is occurring at this moment?The signed oscillating curve
Amplitude scale A(t)How large can that oscillation be near this time?The upper and lower envelope
Frequency f(t)How many complete cycles occur per second?The spacing between successive peaks

The program combines these as

h(t)=A(t)cos⁡Φ(t),dΦdt=2πf(t).

Phase Φ counts progress through the oscillation in radians. An increase of 2π is one complete cycle. Amplitude changes the height of a cycle; frequency changes its duration. The markers above have a fixed amplitude and frequency. The binary signal we will calculate has both changing.

Experiments that go with this beat: EXP-1 · EXP-2 in Suggested Experiments.

Beat 1 · Describe the moving mass distribution

Newtonian physics already gives us tools for describing extended distributions of mass. Total mass answers “how much?” The center of mass answers “where is its balance point?” Second mass moments describe how the mass is spread around that point. Their units are mass times distance squared, as for a moment of inertia.

Place equal masses m at opposite ends of a dumbbell, each a distance b from the center. The separation between the masses is 2b. Use axes fixed on the page, with the center of mass at their origin. Two useful combinations of second mass moments are

Qc=∑imi(xi2−yi2),Qs=2∑imixiyi.

These are two components of the mass quadrupole description. They compare extension along different directions. They are not the total mass and need not be positive. We do not need the complete three-dimensional quadrupole tensor for this planar example.

Qc/(2mb²) = 1.00; Qs/(2mb²) = 0.00. Follow both components as the dumbbell turns.

A short interval with fixed separation and constant rotation rate is assumed here. The line is a visual aid: a binary’s components are held in orbit by gravity, not by a rod.

Try before reading on. Calculate Qc for a horizontal dumbbell and a vertical one. Then double b without changing either mass. By what factor do the nonzero quadrupole components change? At 45°, is Qc = 0 evidence that the dumbbell has become spherical?

For the horizontal arrangement, Qc=2mb2; for the vertical arrangement it is −2mb2. At 45° the x and y extensions match, so Qc=0, but Qs is nonzero. A single component can vanish because of the choice of axes.

If the dumbbell rotates with orbital angle θ, then

Qc=2mb2cos⁡(2θ),Qs=2mb2sin⁡(2θ).

During half a revolution, the two equal masses exchange positions and the mass distribution repeats. Both quadrupole components complete a full cycle in that time. For the leading quadrupole radiation of a circular binary,

fGW=2forb.

We will use f for gravitational-wave frequency throughout the program exercises. An unequal-mass binary has different distances from each body to the center of mass, but its leading circular quadrupole still varies at twice the orbital frequency.

A quadrupole need not radiate

An oblate planet has a different mass distribution along its rotation axis and across its equator. A tidal bulge supplies another familiar example of nonspherical mass structure. These can have nonzero quadrupole moments. But a stationary quadrupole produces no gravitational waves. An axisymmetric oblate planet spinning steadily about its symmetry axis has an unchanging mass distribution: the individual particles move, while the distribution’s quadrupole remains fixed.

For contrast, the rotating dumbbell changes its quadrupole relative to fixed axes. A sphere expanding and contracting while remaining exactly spherical does not create this quadrupolar changing shape. Motion alone is insufficient; the changing distribution matters.

Experiments that go with this beat: EXP-3 in Suggested Experiments.

Beat 2 · Why is the received strain so small?

The quadrupole components have Newtonian meanings. The connection from their motion to an outgoing gravitational wave comes from general relativity. At leading order for a slowly moving source, the radiative strain depends on the second time derivative of its quadrupole. Faster variation matters, not simply a large static distortion.

An order-of-magnitude version of the strain relation is

h∼Gc4DQ¨.

Here D is the source distance and Q¨=d2Q/dt2. The symbol ∼ means that numerical factors, tensor components and viewing-direction factors have been suppressed. This estimates radiation far from a source whose size is small compared with the wavelength; it is not a formula for its nearby static gravitational field.

Check the dimensions
[Q]=kgm2,[Q¨]=kgm2s−2,[Gc4D]=s2kgm2.

The product is dimensionless, as strain must be. This checks the proposed physical formula; dimensional analysis alone does not prove that the quadrupole’s second derivative supplies the radiation.

A useful source scale comes from the circular binary itself. Let a denote the full separation between its bodies, M=m1+m2 their total mass, and

μ=m1m2M

their reduced mass. It is the effective mass that appears when describing their relative motion. For equal component masses m, μ=m/2. The quadrupole scale is Q∼μa2. If the orbital angular frequency is Ω, then Q¨∼μa2Ω2. With relative orbital speed vrel=aΩ,

h∼Gμc2D(vrelc)2.

Now both factors are dimensionless. The first compares the reduced mass’s gravitational length Gμ/c2 with the distance to the observer. The second compares orbital speed with light speed. For distant sources, the first is extremely small; slow motion makes the second small too.

For scale, the 36 + 29 solar-mass example at 440 Mpc has μ≃16.1M⊙, so Gμ/(c2D)≃1.75×10−21. At a wave frequency of 30 Hz, Newtonian circular dynamics gives vrel/c≃0.31. Their product gives an order-of-magnitude strain ∼1.7×10−22. The program’s face-on amplitude includes a factor of four, giving about 6.8×10−22. The rough estimate has identified the physical scale without pretending to reproduce every coefficient.

A small strain at Earth does not imply a low-power source. It describes the tiny fractional deformation produced here after radiation has propagated across an enormous distance.

Try before reading on. Keep the binary unchanged and double D. What should happen to the strain amplitude? Should that alter the source’s orbital history? Make the prediction now; test it in EXP-4.

Experiments that go with this beat: EXP-4 in Suggested Experiments.

Beat 3 · Build the chirp from energy loss and Kepler’s law

A binary emits energy in gravitational waves. Why does its orbit speed up instead of slow down? Resolve that apparent puzzle before using a frequency-evolution formula.

First, compare circular orbits

Consider a sequence of circular Newtonian orbits with the same component masses and different separations a. Let the potential energy be zero at infinite separation. The kinetic, potential and total orbital energies are

K=Gm1m22a,U=−Gm1m2a,Eorb=K+U=−Gm1m22a.

The negative total energy identifies a bound orbit. A more negative value means that more energy would have to be supplied to separate the bodies to infinity. The energies here refer to orbital motion and mutual gravity; they do not include the bodies’ rest-mass energies.

Choose a reference separation a0 and define the positive energy scale E0=Gm1m2/(2a0). At a=a0, the three energies, in units of E0, are K=+1, U=−2, and Eorb=−1.

In units of E₀: K = +1.00, U = -2.00, E = -1.00. Relative speed / reference speed = 1.00; frequency / reference frequency = 1.00.

This compares a family of Newtonian circular orbits with the same component masses; it does not animate their time evolution. E₀ is a positive reference energy. For use as an inspiral picture, the changes must be slow compared with an orbit and the bodies well separated.

Try before reading on. Before selecting “half the separation,” predict K, U and E in units of E₀. Can kinetic energy increase while the total energy decreases? Which contribution must change more?

At half the separation, the values are +2,−4,−2. The kinetic energy has risen by E0, but the potential energy has fallen by 2E0. Their sum has fallen by E0. That net decrease is the energy available to be carried away as radiation while the binary moves between these circular configurations.

Losing total orbital energy and gaining orbital speed are compatible. A tighter bound orbit has a lower total energy and a higher kinetic energy.

Next, use Kepler’s law to predict the frequency

For the relative circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration. Kepler’s third law gives

Ω2=GMa3,forb=Ω2π,f=2forb=1πGMa3.

All distances in these equations use the full body-to-body separation a, not one component’s distance from the center of mass. The relative speed is vrel=GM/a.

At fixed masses, halving a raises the relative speed by 2 and raises both orbital and wave frequencies by 23/2≃2.83. The frequency rises because the binary is following progressively tighter orbits.

Finally, let radiation connect the orbits

The program assumes a quasi-circular inspiral: during the early inspiral the separation changes little in one orbit, so each short interval can be approximated by a circular orbit. Energy and angular momentum carried away by gravitational radiation allow that orbit to shrink. This is not a calculation in which we simply reduce the bodies’ speeds while holding their positions fixed.

Writing PGW>0 for the total power emitted in waves, conservation of energy gives

dEorbdt=−PGW.

Because Eorb=−Gm1m2/(2a), its derivative is

dEorbdt=Gm1m22a2dadt.

The coefficient multiplying da/dt is positive. The energy derivative is negative. Therefore da/dt<0: the separation decreases. Kepler’s law then requires df/dt>0. These signs explain the direction of the chirp before any long coefficient appears.

The quadrupole luminosity of a circular binary gives the strength of the feedback:

PGW=325G4μ2M3c5a5.

At fixed masses, halving the separation increases this leading-order radiated power by a factor of 32. The tighter binary loses energy more rapidly, so its orbital evolution accelerates. Within the same approximation, its strain amplitude at a fixed distance grows as 1/a, so the oscillations also grow taller. These scalings apply to the model’s gradual inspiral, not to a physical merger obtained by taking a to zero.

Follow the algebra from energy balance to the program’s chirp equation

Substituting the radiated power into the energy derivative gives

dadt=−645G3μM2c5a3.

Differentiating f∝a−3/2 at fixed masses gives

dfdt=−3f2adadt.

Eliminate a using a3=GM/(πf)2. The mass dependence groups into μM2/3=M5/3, where M is the chirp mass:

M=μ3/5M2/5=(m1m2)3/5(m1+m2)1/5.

The result is exactly the leading-order equation integrated by the program:

dfdt=965π8/3(GMc3)5/3f11/3.

The steep frequency dependence is the quantitative form of the feedback we just described. At the same masses, doubling f makes this instantaneous sweep rate about 211/3≃12.7 times larger.

We can now account for both visible changes: energy loss tightens the orbit, increasing frequency; the faster-changing quadrupole increases the strain amplitude. On the waveform panel, successive cycles become closer together while the envelope expands.

Beat 4 · Read the program’s chirp

Use Python 3.10 or later with NumPy and Matplotlib. In the program folder containing main.py, check the version:

python main.py --version

For a first figure, use the short black-hole-binary example below. The full 36 + 29 solar-mass run contains few enough cycles to inspect on one screen. Ringdown is left off while we learn the inspiral.

python main.py --m1 36 --m2 29 --d 440 --outdir ./figures

The masses are entered in solar masses and distance in Mpc. The default starting wave frequency is 20 Hz and the default numerical timestep is 0.0002 s. The program displays the figure and also saves a PNG because --outdir is specified.

The printed chirp mass is about 28.0956 solar masses. The modeled sweep lasts about 0.813 seconds, ending at 67.6 Hz with an amplitude scale 1.165×10−21.

Start with the top panel. Compare the distance between neighboring peaks early and late. The dashed lines are +A(t) and −A(t), not additional waves. Panel 2 repeats the positive amplitude scale on its own axis so its growth is easier to inspect. Panel 3 shows the wave frequency directly.

Plot tip: In a Matplotlib window, hovering over the graph displays cursor coordinates in the toolbar. Zoom into a short interval to measure successive peaks. Compare positive peaks with the next positive peaks, rather than with the intervening negative troughs.

Try before reading on. Find an interval where the bottom panel reads roughly 40 Hz. Estimate the duration of one full cycle there. Which two panels let you check the same estimate in different ways?

The time axis starts when the calculation reaches the selected starting frequency. It is not the binary’s age. Likewise, the final printed “time to ISCO” is the duration of this selected frequency interval.

For comparison, python main.py uses 1.4 + 1.4 solar masses at 400 Mpc from 20 Hz. Its roughly 158-second overview compresses many oscillations into one screen width. A dense-looking late trace does not by itself mean the oscillations have disappeared or the numerical data have become random.

What does the program actually calculate?
  1. From the two input masses, calculate total mass and chirp mass.
  2. Use the chirp equation to advance wave frequency, and advance phase with dΦ/dt=2πf.
  3. Calculate A(f), then form h=Acos⁡Φ.
  4. Stop the inspiral at the adopted ISCO frequency.
  5. If requested, append the separate illustrative ringdown.

This is not an N-body integration of two position vectors with a radiation force. The separation discussed in Beat 3 is the circular-orbit interpretation behind the frequency equation. One could reconstruct an approximate separation from f and Kepler’s law; the shipped program does not plot that orbit.

Beat 5 · Give each control a physical question

Move the observer, keeping the source unchanged

Compare the first run with

python main.py --m1 36 --m2 29 --d 880 --outdir ./figures

Only the distance has changed. Predict the effect before running it. Compare the printed amplitude scales rather than the apparent heights in separately autoscaled windows. The model includes inverse-distance amplitude dilution, while cosmological redshift is absent. Consequently changing distance here changes neither the frequency history nor its duration.

From strain sensitivity to detection distance and volume

Inverse-distance scaling has an important observational payoff. For an otherwise unchanged source and viewing geometry, doubling its distance halves the amplitude of the entire waveform. A detector able to recognize the same signal at half the previous amplitude can therefore detect it twice as far away, using the same detection criterion.

Call this improvement in amplitude sensitivity s. If the minimum detectable waveform amplitude falls by a factor s, the detection reach grows by that factor:

Dmax,newDmax,old=s.

In a nearby, approximately Euclidean region of space, the volume inside a detection distance is proportional to its cube:

V=4π3Dmax3,VnewVold=s3.

Twice the reach therefore means eight times the accessible volume. A tenfold improvement in amplitude sensitivity would give ten times the reach and approximately 1,000 times the volume. The sensitivity slider below changes the detector’s ability to recognize a weaker received waveform.

Minimum detectable amplitude: 1.000 of reference; reach: 1.00×; accessible volume: 1.000×.

The circle shows a two-dimensional slice: its radius illustrates detection distance. The bar represents the volume of the corresponding three-dimensional sphere, not the circle’s area. Source type, viewing geometry, observing time and detection criterion are held fixed.

If comparable events occur at a roughly uniform rate per unit volume, the expected number detected in a fixed observing time grows with this volume. Eight times the accessible volume then means approximately eight times the expected detections. This is why even a modest sensitivity improvement can make a substantial difference.

Strain amplitude and energy flux scale differently

The wave’s energy is still spreading over larger spherical surfaces. For the same emitted waveform, the cycle-averaged energy flux (power received per unit area) scales as the square of its strain amplitude:

A∝D−1,FGW∝A2∝D−2.

At twice the distance the strain amplitude is halved and the energy flux is quartered. The inverse-first-power strain law and inverse-square energy-flux law describe different quantities and are consistent with one another.

This is an idealized reach-and-volume argument, not a detection simulation. Real sensitivity depends on noise across the waveform’s frequencies and on source orientation and sky position. At cosmological distances, luminosity distance cannot simply be cubed to obtain surveyed volume. The program models inverse-distance amplitude scaling but does not calculate detector noise, detection probabilities or event rates.

Start following the same evolution later

python main.py --m1 36 --m2 29 --d 440 --f_start 40 --outdir ./figures

This begins at 40 Hz instead of 20 Hz. It does not create a different pair of masses. Its shorter time axis describes the later part of the same leading-order frequency evolution. An arbitrary initial phase is reset at the start, so align waveforms in frequency or time remaining rather than expecting their raw signed samples to match.

Hold total mass fixed and change its division

python main.py --m1 20 --m2 20 --d 440 --outdir ./figures
python main.py --m1 30 --m2 10 --d 440 --outdir ./figures

Both binaries have total mass 40M⊙. At a given separation they therefore have the same Keplerian relative orbital frequency. But their reduced masses differ, which changes both orbital energy and radiated power. Their frequency evolution is not identical.

The mass combination that organizes the leading sweep is the chirp mass:

M=(m1m2)3/5(m1+m2)1/5.

At the same wave frequency, larger chirp mass gives a faster sweep and a larger face-on amplitude at fixed distance. Chirp mass is not another object in the binary; it is a combination of the two masses. The total mass will set the program’s cutoff, while chirp mass sets the leading sweep.

The complete face-on amplitude scale used in the program is

A(f)=4(GM)5/3(πf)2/3c4D.

You already know its main features: inverse distance, a growing amplitude as the orbit tightens, and dependence on the participating masses. The equation supplies precise coefficients within the approximation.

Beat 6 · Why does the inspiral stop?

Kepler’s law and the Newtonian energy formula do not tell us where a relativistic compact binary merges. Continuing those approximations to arbitrarily small separation would go beyond their domain of validity.

General relativity provides a useful strong-field benchmark. For a test particle orbiting a nonrotating black hole, circular orbits outside the innermost stable circular orbit, or ISCO, are stable against small radial disturbances. ISCO is the marginal boundary. Between it and the photon sphere there are circular massive-particle orbits, but they are unstable.

Stability matters because an orbit can exist mathematically yet fail to retain a particle after a small disturbance. The ISCO is not the event horizon and not the photon sphere. For a Schwarzschild black hole,

rH=2GMc2,rph=3GMc2,rISCO=6GMc2.

The photon sphere concerns circular light motion; its circular orbit is unstable. ISCO concerns the stability of massive-particle circular motion. In idealized thin accretion-disk models, this loss of stable circular orbits also helps identify the inner disk region. We do not need a disk model to use the orbital distinction here.

For the Schwarzschild circular-orbit frequency measured by a distant observer, the associated dominant wave frequency at ISCO is

fISCO=c363/2πGM.

The program substitutes the binary’s total mass for M and adopts this as its cutoff. The test-particle formula is not an exact endpoint for two comparable masses. Nor does it determine the physical merger of the default neutron-star binary, for which matter and tidal effects can matter.

The vertical line says “this approximate inspiral calculation ends here.” It does not say “a complete merger calculation predicts this exact time.”

Try before reading on. If both component masses double while the mass ratio stays fixed, what happens to this adopted cutoff frequency? Explain using the formula before checking the printed values.

Experiments that go with this beat: EXP-7 · EXP-11 in Suggested Experiments.

Beat 7 · Add an illustrative ringdown

A disturbed black hole can relax by emitting damped oscillations, called quasi-normal modes. This gives a different physical picture from two bodies circling one another: one remnant is settling toward equilibrium.

Request the program’s simplified example:

python main.py --m1 36 --m2 29 --d 440 --ringdown --t_before 0.2 --t_after 0.05 --outdir ./figures

In the saved figure the annotation box hides the top of the first ringdown peak. In the Matplotlib window, zoom to roughly 0.812–0.834 s to see the join and the first ringdown cycles before measuring periods.

A damped sinusoid has an oscillation frequency and an exponentially shrinking envelope. If u is time since the ringdown begins, its envelope decreases as e−u/τ. At one decay time τ the envelope is 1/e of its initial value; at two it is 1/e2. That does not require every signed sample or every neighboring absolute peak to have exactly those ratios.

For this illustration, the program assumes Mf=0.95(m1+m2) and a nonrotating remnant. It reports fQNM=195.5Hz and τ=3.417ms. It joins the strain and phase at the cutoff, but does not calculate a physical merger or enforce a physical energy-flux match there.

The simplification matters: realistic black-hole-binary remnants generally spin, while a neutron-star merger need not immediately produce a black hole. The red extension illustrates damped ringing under the stated assumptions.

Where do its frequency and decay time come from?

The fundamental quadrupolar Schwarzschild mode is represented by the dimensionless complex angular frequency

GMfc3ω≃0.3737−0.0890i.

Its real part gives oscillation and its negative imaginary part gives decay. In ordinary units the program uses

fQNM=0.37372πc3GMf,τ=GMf0.0890c3.

At the same assumed spin, increasing remnant mass lowers frequency and lengthens the decay time. The numerical constants are imported results of relativistic perturbation theory; they are not derived by this tutorial.

Suggested Experiments

The links after each Beat lead to exercises that use its ideas. Make predictions before running comparisons; keep a small table of inputs and printed quantities. The final experiment is optional computational work.

EXP-1

Read the three panels

Use the Beat 4 command. Select early and late intervals. Describe separately how cycle spacing and envelope height change, and identify the panel that displays each change directly. Explain what a negative value in the waveform means using the receiving markers.

Back to experiments

EXP-2

Measure a period in two ways

In the Beat 4 figure, choose a short interval in which f changes little. Estimate a full period from neighboring positive peaks and compare its inverse with the frequency panel near the interval’s midpoint. Explain why a long interval gives a less local comparison.

Back to experiments

EXP-3

Which changing distributions can radiate?

Use the dumbbell calculation to predict the quadrupole change if both masses double, or if their distance from the center doubles. Compare a stationary dumbbell, a rotating dumbbell, and an axisymmetric oblate planet spinning about its symmetry axis. State which have a changing quadrupole in fixed axes and explain your reasoning.

Back to experiments

EXP-4

Separate propagation from source evolution

Compare the 440-Mpc and 880-Mpc runs of Beat 5. Record the printed amplitude scale, duration and cutoff frequency. Test inverse-distance scaling quantitatively. Explain why two autoscaled waveform windows can look nearly identical even when their numerical amplitudes differ. Then suppose a detector could recognize the same waveform at two-thirds of its previous minimum amplitude. Before using the sensitivity slider, calculate the factors by which detection distance and accessible volume would increase. What change in expected detection rate would follow for a roughly uniform event rate per unit volume and the same observing time? State which assumptions make that estimate possible.

Back to experiments

EXP-5

Account for the energy

Starting from a circular orbit at separation a₀, compare one at a₀/2. Express the change in kinetic energy, potential energy and total orbital energy in units of E₀. How much positive energy could be carried away in the gradual transition? Then use Kepler’s law to find the speed and frequency ratios. Explain how all of these changes can occur together.

Back to experiments

EXP-6

Follow the same binary from a later point

Compare the 20-Hz and 40-Hz starts for the 36 + 29 solar-mass binary. Subtract the printed durations to estimate time spent between 20 and 40 Hz. Is that the same duration as the remaining 40-Hz-to-cutoff portion? Use the accelerating sweep to explain the difference. The phase origin is reset in each run, so compare f and A at matched frequency rather than raw h at the same elapsed time.

Back to experiments

EXP-7

Divide a fixed total mass differently

Compare 20 + 20, 25 + 15, and 30 + 10 solar masses, all at 440 Mpc from 20 Hz. Tabulate total mass, chirp mass, duration, cutoff frequency and cutoff amplitude. Which quantity stays fixed, and which changes? Use the distinction between total and chirp mass to explain the results.

Back to experiments

EXP-8

Infer chirp mass from the sweep

Run python main.py --f_start 100 --csvdir ./data. This uses the default 1.4 + 1.4 solar-mass binary, but starts later to keep the CSV small. Data rows follow the commented metadata and header. Take two rows near the start, separated by about 0.002 s. Estimate df/dt from their frequency difference divided by their time difference, and evaluate it at their mean frequency. Rearrange the chirp equation, or use physics_gw.chirp_mass_from_fdot(f_mid, fdot_est), to infer chirp mass. The helper returns kilograms: divide by physics_gw.M_sun for solar masses. To use it, start Python by entering python in the folder containing main.py. At the Python prompt, enter import physics_gw as p, assign your estimated mean frequency in Hz to f_mid and slope in Hz/s to fdot_est, then evaluate p.chirp_mass_from_fdot(f_mid, fdot_est) / p.M_sun. Compare with the printed 1.2188 solar masses. Repeat with wider separation between rows and consider the effect of estimating a derivative across a changing slope. This is an inverse exercise using noiseless model output, not an independent observational validation.

Back to experiments

EXP-9

Measure damped ringing

Use the Beat 7 command. In the Matplotlib window, zoom to roughly 0.812–0.834 s so the annotation box no longer hides the first ringdown peak. Measure several ringdown periods and compare the estimated frequency with the printed value. Separately, use the decay time to predict the envelope after one and two decay times. Explain why comparing samples of opposite phase is not a measurement of envelope decay.

Back to experiments

EXP-10

Scale the remnant

Run equal-mass examples 20 + 20 and 40 + 40 solar masses with --ringdown --f_start 20, keeping the same distance. Test whether doubling the assumed remnant mass halves QNM frequency and doubles decay time. Do the same ratios hold for the program’s adopted ISCO frequency? Distinguish the physical meanings of these two frequencies.

Back to experiments

EXP-11

Identify the calculation’s boundary

Using the figure and Help, identify which portions are calculated from the leading-order inspiral equation and which are prescribed separately. Explain why the cutoff is neither the horizon nor the photon sphere. Make an included/omitted list covering circularity, spins, detector response, cosmological redshift, tides and merger dynamics. You are identifying the assumptions, not being asked to quantify effects that this tutorial has not calculated.

Back to experiments

EXP-12

Optional numerical investigation

For the 36 + 29 solar-mass example, export CSV files using timesteps 0.0064, 0.0032, 0.0016 and 0.0008 s. Compare f at the fixed interior time 0.7680 s, which is a nominal sample time in all four runs and precedes every cutoff. Select the row nearest that time: repeated floating-point additions may make its recorded time differ from 0.7680 in the last few digits. How many frequency digits settle as the timestep is reduced? The terminal rounds the cutoff time to 0.813 s in every run, so compare instead the time in the final data row of each CSV, which is the interpolated cutoff. Do successive differences of that endpoint time shrink by the same factor as the interior frequency differences? Relate what you find to the program’s linearly interpolated final crossing step. These checks investigate numerical sensitivity; do not assume that every successive difference must have an exact ratio of 16. Very small steps at an early comparison time can already make frequency differences too small to distinguish cleanly from floating-point rounding. The CSV retains the precision needed for this comparison; plot smoothness is insufficient.

Back to experiments

Reference · Equations and controls

How long does a selected frequency interval last?

Integrating the leading-order chirp equation between wave frequencies f1 and f2 gives

Δt=5256π8/3(GMc3)−5/3(f1−8/3−f2−8/3).

The duration is dominated by the lower-frequency portion when f1≪f2. It is the duration of a selected interval, not the system’s age. A near-power-law dependence on starting frequency is therefore expected, with a finite endpoint correction.

OptionDefaultMeaning
--m1, --m21.4, 1.4Component masses in solar masses
--d400Distance in Mpc; amplitude dilution only in this model
--f_start20Starting gravitational-wave frequency in Hz, below the adopted cutoff
--dt0.0002Integration timestep in seconds; also controls inspiral sample spacing
--ringdownoffAdd the illustrative nonrotating-remnant ringdown
--n_tau, --rd_pts6, 4000Ringdown duration in decay times and number of ringdown points; jointly checked for at least 8 samples per cycle
--t_before, --t_afterfull available intervalDisplay windows in seconds before and after the cutoff; change neither numerical evolution nor exported data
--outdirno saveSave a timestamped PNG in addition to displaying the figure
--csvdirno exportExport numerical samples and metadata to a timestamped CSV
--lw, --dpi0.4, 150Waveform line width and saved PNG resolution (1 through 600 dpi)

python main.py --help lists current options and bounds. The numerical timestep must resolve the fastest oscillations; satisfying the input checks is not itself a precision guarantee.

CSV columns are t_s,f_hz,A,h,phase_rad. Metadata above the header identifies the run. Inspiral f and A entries are blank in the appended ringdown, which has its own frequency and decaying envelope. A default 20-Hz neutron-star example produces roughly 789,000 rows; the 100-Hz start in EXP-8 produces about 10,800.

Numerical comparisons should use the program’s own constants: G=6.67430×10−11m3kg−1s−2, c=299792458ms−1, and 1Mpc=3.08567758149×1022m. Its solar-mass unit is calculated as M⊙=(1.3271244×1020m3s−2)/G, with the nominal solar gravitational parameter in the numerator.

What this model includes—and what it leaves for later

The calculation supplies a leading-order, quasi-circular inspiral, a face-on amplitude scale, and an optional prescribed nonrotating-black-hole ringdown. It does not supply a detector antenna pattern, inclination dependence, cosmological redshift, eccentricity, spins, tides, higher harmonics, a relativistic merger, or a self-consistently predicted remnant.

Newtonian circular energy and Kepler’s law explain the early inspiral particularly well. Corrections become important toward the strong-field endpoint. Neither the extrapolated Newtonian orbit nor the adopted cutoff is a substitute for a full merger calculation.

There is considerable physics to explore within those limits: receiving strain, changing mass moments, the energy budget of shrinking orbits, the accelerating sweep, the roles of two different mass combinations, inverse-distance scaling and damped ringing.

Further reading and provenance

The text and adjustable diagrams develop the elementary relations explicitly, starting from the supplied program. Program figures were regenerated from version 1.8.0. No measured waveform or detector data are presented.

  • Markus Pössel, “The wave nature of simple gravitational waves,” Einstein Online — a complementary explanation of receiving markers and propagation.
  • LIGO Scientific and Virgo Collaborations, “The basic physics of the binary black hole merger GW150914” — an elementary analysis of a real event; Appendix A develops the circular-binary energy-balance argument.
  • Barack and Sago, “Gravitational self-force correction to the innermost stable circular orbit of a Schwarzschild black hole” — an advanced reference identifying the Schwarzschild test-particle ISCO and corrections beyond that limit.
  • Chen et al., “Distance measures in gravitational-wave astrophysics and cosmology” — detection reach, sensitive volume and the qualifications needed at cosmological distances.
